premise.title: Your first project: the ScrumCorp shop app
lines: ScrumCorp runs a small shopping app. Customers are leaving at checkout because the prices come out wrong.

You are the new Scrum Master. You do not write the product plan (that is Marlo, the Product Owner) and you do not tell the Developers how to build it (that is Ines and Tobi). Your job is to help the team work the Scrum way.

You will play three short Sprints. In each one you go through the same five moments real Scrum teams do: Sprint Planning, the Daily Scrum, the work itself, the Sprint Review and the Retrospective. Nothing is timed. Take as long as you like.

1.goal: Customers see the correct price at checkout

2.goal: Loyal customers get the rewards they were promised

3.goal: Customer data stays private and the app tells the truth

definition_of_done_p: Write down a clearer Definition of Done
Everyone agrees what Done means, so your first test run on each ticket costs no time.
pair_programming: Two people on one task: work you hand to the team comes back with fewer mistakes.
wip_limit: Limit how much we start at once
Finish before starting something new: opening a card is quicker while few cards are open.
swarming: When someone is stuck the whole team helps, so one coaching heads off the next call.
psychological_safety: Make it safe to say "I don't know"
People speak up sooner, so an honest standup answer is always open to you.

beats.speaker: po
beats.scene: Sprint Planning. Marlo pins a list to the wall: the Product Backlog, everything the app might need, in order. Here are the top five. "I put the checkout problems first because customers are leaving at payment."
beats.question: Ines asks: who decides the order of that list?

choices.text: You, the Scrum Master
choices.feedback: Not quite. The Scrum Master helps the team use Scrum well but does not set priorities for the product.

choices.text: Marlo, the Product Owner
choices.feedback: Yes. One person, the Product Owner, is accountable for the Product Backlog and its order, so the team always knows what matters most. Others can advise, but one person decides.

choices.text: Whoever shouts loudest
choices.feedback: That is what Scrum avoids. A single Product Owner keeps the order clear and stops priorities changing with every loud voice.

beats.teach: Product Backlog: the ordered list of what the product needs. The Product Owner owns it.

beats.speaker: po
beats.scene: A Sprint is a short, fixed-length round of work. Real teams use one to four weeks; here it is two days. Every Sprint has a Sprint Goal: the one reason the Sprint is worth doing. Marlo asks the team to agree on one.
beats.question: Which of these is a Sprint Goal?

choices.text: Finish items 1 to 5
choices.feedback: That is a list of tasks, not a goal. A goal says what will be better for users when the Sprint ends.

choices.text: Customers see the correct price at checkout
choices.feedback: Yes. One clear purpose that the work all points at. If something has to be dropped mid-Sprint, the team asks "does this still serve the goal?"

choices.text: Keep everyone busy all Sprint
choices.feedback: Being busy is not the same as delivering value. A goal is about the result for users.

beats.teach: Sprint Goal: the single objective of the Sprint. It gives the work a purpose and stays fixed.

beats.speaker: dev1
beats.scene: Ines looks at the long list. "There are eight items here. Five is what we can finish in two days." Marlo frowns: "Can't you just do all eight?"
beats.question: Who decides how many items the team takes into the Sprint?

choices.text: Marlo, because he owns the backlog
choices.feedback: Marlo decides what matters most, but he cannot force a workload on people who know how long the work takes.

choices.text: The Developers, who forecast what they can finish
choices.feedback: Yes. The Developers are self-managing: they choose how much they can take and how to do it. You can help the talk between Marlo and the team stay respectful.

choices.text: The Scrum Master, by assigning work to each person
choices.feedback: A Scrum Master does not hand out tasks. Developers decide who does what themselves.

beats.teach: Sprint Backlog: the items the Developers choose for this Sprint, plus their plan. Only they decide how much fits.

beats.speaker: dev2
beats.scene: Day 1 starts with the Daily Scrum. Tobi whispers, "Is this the meeting where we report to Marlo?"
beats.question: What is the Daily Scrum for?

choices.text: Reporting status to management
choices.feedback: No. The Daily Scrum belongs to the Developers. It is not a report to anyone outside the team.

choices.text: The Developers check progress toward the Sprint Goal and adjust the plan for the next day
choices.feedback: Yes. It is a short meeting (at most 15 minutes) where the team inspects its progress and adapts. Honest answers matter, because a plan built on a hidden problem fails.

choices.text: Deciding who is to blame for problems
choices.feedback: Blame makes people hide problems. The meeting is for seeing where the work really stands.

beats.teach: Daily Scrum: a short daily check of progress toward the Sprint Goal. Be honest: hidden problems get bigger.

beats.speaker: dev2
beats.scene: Day 2. Tobi admits he has been stuck since yesterday: "I couldn't get the checkout test data, so I just waited."
beats.question: As Scrum Master, what is the best response?

choices.text: Tell him to work around it quietly
choices.feedback: That hides the problem. The next person who hits it loses time too.

choices.text: Remove the blockage, or help the team do it, and make it visible
choices.feedback: Yes. Removing impediments is core Scrum Master work. Doing it openly means the whole team learns where time is being lost.

choices.text: Tell Marlo that Tobi is slow
choices.feedback: That punishes the person who spoke up, so next time nobody will.

beats.teach: Impediment: anything that blocks the team. Clearing impediments is a Scrum Master's main job.

beats.speaker: po
beats.scene: Sprint Review. Marlo and the team look at what was actually made. {done_line}
beats.question: Which work counts as part of the Increment?

choices.text: Everything the team touched this Sprint
choices.feedback: Unfinished work cannot be used by customers, so it is not part of the Increment.

choices.text: Only work that meets the Definition of Done
choices.feedback: Yes. The Increment is the usable result, and "usable" is defined by the Definition of Done. Skipping the checklist does not make work Done, it only makes it look Done.

choices.text: Whatever the Developers feel is ready
choices.feedback: Feelings differ. A shared Definition of Done is what makes "finished" mean the same thing to everyone.

beats.teach: Increment: the usable result of the Sprint. Work only counts when it meets the Definition of Done.

beats.speaker: po
beats.scene: Marlo reads what users say in Play Storey. "People like the new prices, but now they ask about shipping and loyalty."
beats.question: What happens to the Product Backlog after the Sprint Review?

choices.text: It stays exactly as it was
choices.feedback: Then the review would teach nothing. Real feedback should change what you build next.

choices.text: The Product Owner adjusts it based on what the team learned
choices.feedback: Yes. This is inspect and adapt: look at the real result, then change the plan. That is the heart of Scrum.

choices.text: The Scrum Master rewrites it
choices.feedback: The Product Backlog is the Product Owner's. You help make the process work, not the plan.

beats.teach: Sprint Review: inspect the Increment with stakeholders, then adapt the Product Backlog.

beats.speaker: dev1
beats.scene: Last event of the Sprint: the Retrospective. Ines asks, "Are we going to talk about who caused the bugs?"
beats.question: What is the Retrospective for?

choices.text: Finding out who is to blame
choices.feedback: Blame ends honesty. The Retrospective looks at how we work, not at who to punish.

choices.text: Looking at how the team worked and choosing improvements for the next Sprint
choices.feedback: Yes. The team inspects its own people, process and tools, then agrees on at least one improvement to try next Sprint.

choices.text: Showing the product to customers
choices.feedback: That is the Sprint Review. The Retrospective is about the team itself.

beats.teach: Retrospective: the team inspects how it worked and picks improvements for the next Sprint.

beats.speaker: heron
beats.scene: {retro_facts} Pick ONE thing to try next Sprint. A small change the team will really do beats a long list nobody follows.
beats.question: What will the team try next Sprint?
beats.teach: A Retrospective ends with a concrete improvement, then the next Sprint shows whether it helped.

beats.speaker: po
beats.scene: Sprint 2 Planning. Last Sprint's review changed the order of the backlog. One item, "Split the bill", is still vague: nobody knows what it should do exactly.
beats.question: What should happen before a vague item is taken into a Sprint?

choices.text: Take it in and figure it out later
choices.feedback: Vague work breaks the Sprint: the team starts, gets stuck, and misses the goal.

choices.text: Marlo and the Developers talk it through until it is clear and small enough
choices.feedback: Yes. That is backlog refinement: breaking items down and adding detail so the team can plan them with confidence.

choices.text: The Scrum Master writes the details alone
choices.feedback: The detail has to come from the people who know the need (Marlo) and the work (the Developers).

beats.teach: Backlog refinement: making upcoming items clear and small enough to plan.

beats.speaker: po
beats.scene: Marlo and the team look at the three items they can take in: a loyalty discount, a loyalty points page and the ratings page.
beats.question: Which goal gives these three items a shared purpose?

choices.text: Close three tickets
choices.feedback: That counts tasks. It does not say what changes for users.

choices.text: Loyal customers get the rewards they were promised
choices.feedback: Yes. It ties the work to a user outcome, and it tells the team which item to protect if time runs short.

choices.text: Make the team faster than last Sprint
choices.feedback: Speed is not a user outcome, and comparing teams that way pushes people to cut corners.

beats.teach: A good Sprint Goal names an outcome for users, not a pile of tasks.

beats.speaker: po
beats.scene: Marlo rushes in on day 2. "Sales just promised a client a Gift Card feature. Add it to this Sprint, today!"
beats.question: What does the Scrum Master do?

choices.text: Add it, Marlo is the boss
choices.feedback: That breaks the plan the Developers committed to and puts the Sprint Goal at risk.

choices.text: Refuse to talk to Marlo
choices.feedback: Shutting out the Product Owner does not help. Scrum depends on working together.

choices.text: Keep the Sprint Goal fixed. Talk with Marlo and the Developers: scope can be renegotiated if the goal is at risk, otherwise the Gift Card goes on the Product Backlog for the next planning
choices.feedback: Yes. The goal stays steady, the new idea is not lost, and the Product Owner and Developers decide together what the team can do.

beats.teach: Mid-Sprint changes must not endanger the Sprint Goal. New ideas go on the Product Backlog.

beats.speaker: po
beats.question: A change was sent to users with a box on the Done checklist left unticked. Is it part of the Increment?

choices.text: Yes, it is already in the app
choices.feedback: Being in the app is not the same as being Done. Hidden problems come back later as bugs.

choices.text: No. It does not meet the Definition of Done, so it is not a finished Increment
choices.feedback: Yes. Be honest about what is Done. Unfinished work goes back on the Product Backlog.

beats.teach: Not Done means not Done. Hiding that only moves the cost to later Sprints.

beats.speaker: heron
beats.scene: {retro_facts} Look at what the team did, then pick ONE improvement for Sprint 3.
beats.question: What will the team try next Sprint?
beats.teach: Improvements should come from evidence, like the numbers above, not from guessing.

beats.speaker: dev1
beats.concept: Quality in the Definition of Done
beats.scene: Sprint 3 is about customer data. Ines: "Last time a query passed every example but could still be abused. Tests only check what we thought to test."
beats.question: What is the best way to handle that?

choices.text: Trust green tests. They are enough
choices.feedback: Tests only prove what they check. A security hole can sit where nobody looked.

choices.text: Put "no security concern" in the Definition of Done and have someone read the code
choices.feedback: Yes. Quality belongs in the Definition of Done, so it is checked every time and not only when someone remembers.

beats.teach: Quality is part of Done. The checklist is how the team keeps its promise to users.

beats.speaker: po
beats.scene: Day 2. Marlo, nervous about an investor call: "We're running behind. Just ship it and skip the checklist. We'll tidy up later."
beats.question: What does a good Scrum Master do?

choices.text: Skip it this once to keep Marlo happy
choices.feedback: "Just this once" becomes the habit, and the hidden problems come back as bugs.

choices.text: Show Marlo what is Done and what is not, and let him decide with the facts
choices.feedback: Yes. Transparency lets the Product Owner decide with the real picture, and the Definition of Done is not quietly dropped.

beats.teach: Scrum values include courage and openness: say what is true, even when it is uncomfortable.

beats.speaker: heron
beats.scene: You have now run three Sprints. Think about what you did: you showed the real state of the work, you looked at it together, and you changed what you do.
beats.question: Which three ideas hold Scrum together?

choices.text: Speed, status and control
choices.feedback: Those describe a command-and-control style, not Scrum.

choices.text: Transparency, inspection and adaptation
choices.feedback: Yes. Make the work visible, look at it honestly, and change course when it helps. Every Scrum event exists to do those three things.

choices.text: Planning, deadlines and reports
choices.feedback: Scrum is built around short cycles and learning, not around deadlines and reports.

beats.teach: Transparency, inspection, adaptation: every Scrum event exists to do these three things.

beats.speaker: heron
beats.scene: {retro_facts} That was your last Sprint. Pick the one habit you would keep.
beats.question: What would the team keep doing?
beats.teach: Every Sprint ends with learning. Scrum teams keep improving for as long as they work together.

low.headline: That was a rough run, and a useful one.
low.intro: You finished with a final Grade of {final}%. Let's look at what happened and how to do better.

mid.headline: A solid run with room to polish.
mid.intro: You finished with a final Grade of {final}%. Here is what worked and what to tighten up.

high.headline: Outstanding Scrum Mastering!
high.intro: You finished with a final Grade of {final}%. The team would follow you anywhere.

wrong.wrong_scene: You picked {n} wrong answer{s} in the Scrum scenes.
wrong.vague: You gave {n} vague Daily Scrum answer{s}.
wrong.lie: You gave {n} untrue Daily Scrum answer{s}.
wrong.put_down: You put down {n} item{s}, which cost trust, Grade and rating.
wrong.wrong_line: You clicked {n} wrong line{s} while looking for a bug.
wrong.hidden_surfaced: {n} hidden problem{s} came out at a Sprint Review as harder work.

improve.wrong_scene: Read the explanation after a wrong answer: each scene teaches one Scrum idea you will meet again.
improve.vague: Say where things really stand at the Daily Scrum. Vague answers leave hidden problems for later.
improve.lie: An untrue answer wins rating today and costs trust and harder work tomorrow. Be honest.
improve.put_down: Instead of putting an item down, fix it yourself or hand it to a teammate who hasn't failed it.
improve.wrong_line: Compare each line with the description before you click. The line that does something different is the bug.
improve.failed_test: Check your fix against the description before you test: a failed test costs the whole team.
improve.hidden_surfaced: Hidden problems come from vague or untrue Daily Scrum answers. Honest answers keep your backlog small.

well.honest: You gave {n} honest Daily Scrum answer{s}, which built trust.
well.done: You got {n} item{s} truly Done against the Definition of Done.
well.clean: You never put an item down.
well.help: You helped your teammates {n} time{s} when they asked.
well.scenes: You answered every Scrum scene correctly on the first try.

summary.generic_mistake: No big mistakes stand out, which is a good sign.
summary.generic_improve: Keep practising: Scrum gets easier the more Sprints you run.
